paragraphs: Training a classifier to resist adversarial changes can be much more expensive than ordinary training. Protection against one way of measuring those changes also leaves the question of robustness under other measurements. This paper asks how much existing robust classifiers can gain through a short additional training stage.

The proposed method, Extreme norm Adversarial Training, uses geometric properties of l_p balls to train for multiple threat models. The authors report that it costs up to three times less than other methods for multiple-norm adversarial training. Their experiments show that one epoch on ImageNet and three on CIFAR-10 suffice to convert existing single-norm robust models into multiple-norm robust models.

The work reports the first multiple-norm robust ImageNet model and multiple-norm robustness above 51% on CIFAR-10. It also studies transferring robustness between individual threat models, improving the reported state of the art for l_1 robustness on both datasets. Results across architectures, including vision transformers, support fine-tuning as a practical way to reuse already learned robustness.
icml-2022-adversarial-robustness-against.tldr: Short fine-tuning with Extreme norm Adversarial Training extends existing classifiers’ robustness across multiple perturbation norms.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning infers a reward from an expert’s behavior, often so another learner can subsequently acquire similar behavior. This paper argues that reward selection should consider both compatibility with the expert and how effectively the reward supports that later learning stage when data are limited.

The method jointly selects reward parameters and the discount factor, which controls the importance of future rewards. This creates a trade-off: a potentially suboptimal reward can introduce error, while learning from finitely many samples introduces estimation error. A min-max formulation seeks a robust choice that minimizes the difference between the expert’s policy and the policy learned afterward.

The resulting approach is model-free and does not require solving planning or forward reinforcement learning problems during reward inference. The authors provide a numerical optimization scheme and demonstrate its effectiveness in an illustrative numerical case. The contribution is therefore a formulation that explicitly connects inferred rewards to the practical sample constraints of apprenticeship learning, together with an initial numerical demonstration.
icml-2022-balancing-sample-efficiency-an.tldr: Jointly choosing rewards and a discount factor lets inverse reinforcement learning account for limited data in subsequent policy learning.

paragraphs: Drift detectors typically compare recent deployment data with historical reference data to check whether their distributions differ. That comparison can be misleading when some changes are expected or permitted. For example, the proportions of different subpopulations may change even when the distribution within each subpopulation remains stable.

This paper reframes detection around distributions conditional on context. Instead of treating every difference between batches as relevant drift, it asks whether differences remain after accounting for context that may legitimately vary. The authors adapt tools from causal inference, using two-sample tests for conditional distributional treatment effects, and recommend an implementation based on maximum conditional mean discrepancies.

The empirical study demonstrates usefulness across several practical drift detection problems. In particular, the framework detects distribution changes within subpopulations while remaining insensitive to their relative prevalence. The authors also demonstrate applicability to ImageNet-scale vision tasks. These findings support monitoring that separates changes in the composition of incoming data from changes in the conditional distributions being monitored.
icml-2022-context-aware-drift-detection-.tldr: Context-aware drift detection tests for distribution changes while accounting for contextual variation that is allowed to occur.

paragraphs: Continuous control involves choosing actions from a continuous range, whereas many deep reinforcement learning methods operate on discrete alternatives. Action Quantization from Demonstrations, or AQuaDem, connects these settings by learning a discrete set of action choices from human demonstrations.

The learned discretization depends on the current state. For each input state, it supplies several actions that are plausible in light of the demonstrations. This lets the available choices reflect the demonstrator’s preferences and multimodal behavior: there can be multiple plausible ways to act in the same situation. The discretization therefore carries information about demonstrated behavior into the control problem.

Once actions are represented this way, discrete-action deep reinforcement learning techniques can be applied to the continuous task. The authors report experimental improvements over SAC in reinforcement learning and GAIL in imitation learning. These results support demonstration-based action discretization as a useful interface between continuous environments and discrete learning algorithms, with demonstrations shaping the choices available to the learner.
icml-2022-continuous-control-with-action.tldr: AQuaDem learns state-dependent discrete action choices from demonstrations so discrete reinforcement learning methods can tackle continuous control.

paragraphs: Causal knowledge is often collected in one environment and used in another where some conditions or mechanisms differ. This paper studies that transfer for counterfactual quantities: questions about what would have happened under alternative circumstances. Such questions go beyond describing observed associations or the results of interventions.

The authors consider an arbitrary combination of observational and experimental distributions from different domains. They introduce a graphical condition that is both necessary and sufficient for transporting the target counterfactual within their nonparametric setting. They also develop an efficient algorithm that is sound and complete, tying the graphical characterization to a procedure for obtaining transportable quantities.

Completeness gives algorithmic failure a substantive meaning. Within the stated framework, failure means that the available data cannot determine the target counterfactual without additional assumptions. The contribution therefore addresses both sides of transfer: how to generalize counterfactual knowledge when the information supports it, and how to recognize when that information is insufficient.
icml-2022-counterfactual-transportabilit.tldr: A necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion and complete algorithm determine when counterfactual quantities can be transported across environments.

paragraphs: Given a sequence of numbers, symbolic regression seeks a mathematical rule that explains the observed values. This paper trains Transformers to infer either a function or a recurrence relation underlying sequences of integers or floating-point numbers. The desired output is an explicit mathematical description of how the sequence is generated.

A recurrence describes sequence values through a relationship involving other values, making recurrence prediction a way to recover structure from observations. The authors evaluate their integer model on a subset of the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. On that evaluation, it outperforms Mathematica’s built-in functions for recurrence prediction.

The floating-point model also produces informative approximations for functions and constants outside its vocabulary. The reported examples include approximating a Bessel function with a trigonometric expression and recognizing a numerical constant through an expression involving pi. These findings show that the model can provide useful symbolic descriptions even when the target expression cannot be represented directly using its available vocabulary.
icml-2022-deep-symbolic-regression-for-r.tldr: Transformers infer symbolic functions and recurrences from numerical sequences, including useful approximations for expressions outside their vocabulary.

paragraphs: Conversational question answering needs training examples in which questions develop through an exchange, but collecting such conversations is expensive. Dialog inpainting creates synthetic exchanges from existing documents. It treats document sentences as a writer’s utterances and generates the imagined reader’s questions or comments between them.

Applied to Wikipedia and web passages, the method produces WikiDialog and WebDialog, totaling 19 million information-seeking conversations. The authors describe this as 1,000 times the size of the largest existing conversational question-answering dataset. Human raters judge WikiDialog’s answer adequacy and conversationality to be as good as or better than those of existing manually collected datasets.

The approach also generates high-quality data without in-domain conversational question-answering examples, demonstrating strong zero-shot capability. Pretraining retrieval systems with the generated conversations improves results across QReCC, OR-QuAC, and TREC CAsT, with relative gains reaching 40% on standard metrics. The findings connect the generated data’s conversational quality to measurable benefits for retrieving information during a conversation.
icml-2022-dialog-inpainting-turning-docu.tldr: Dialog inpainting turns documents into synthetic conversations that improve conversational retrieval when used for pretraining.

paragraphs: Vector-quantized variational autoencoders represent inputs using a finite collection of learned embeddings. Generating new examples also requires a distribution over these discrete representations. In the setup described by the authors, that distribution is learned separately with a complex autoregressive model, creating a bottleneck for generation.

This paper replaces the separate training arrangement with a model that learns the prior together with the encoder and decoder. Its central construction is a diffusion bridge connecting a continuous coded vector to a non-informative prior distribution. Discrete latent states are then obtained as random functions of the continuous vectors, linking the discrete representation to the continuous diffusion construction.

The framework extends standard VQ-VAE and permits end-to-end training of the combined system. On mini-ImageNet and CIFAR, the authors report performance competitive with an autoregressive prior, alongside efficient optimization and sampling. The stated result is a practical alternative for learning and generating with discrete latent representations while bringing their component networks into one training process.
icml-2022-diffusion-bridges-vector-quant.tldr: A diffusion bridge enables joint training of a VQ-VAE’s prior, encoder, and decoder with competitive generation and efficient sampling.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives clients tailored models to accommodate differences in their local data. Centralized implementations can concentrate communication demands on a server and make that server a vulnerable point. DisPFL instead organizes personalized learning through direct communication between clients.

The framework uses personalized sparse masks to specify which parameters are active in each local model. Its decentralized sparse training procedure keeps a fixed number of active parameters throughout local training and peer-to-peer communication. Sparsity therefore governs both the models being trained and the information involved in collaboration, addressing computation and communication together.

Experiments show reduced communication pressure on the busiest client, alongside higher accuracy, less computation, and fewer communication rounds. The authors also demonstrate adaptation to clients with different computational capabilities and report improved personalized performance. These findings support combining decentralized exchange with sparse local models as a way to accommodate both differences in client data and differences in available computing resources.
icml-2022-dispfl-towards-communication-e.tldr: DisPFL combines peer-to-peer communication and personalized sparse models to reduce federated learning costs while improving accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Entropic causal inference seeks a causal explanation of observational data by favoring the structural model with the smallest entropy. Earlier work considered two variables. This paper relaxes assumptions for identifying causal structure in that setting and extends the approach to graphs containing more than two nodes.

The key connection is that two-variable entropic tests can determine ancestry between a source node and its descendants. The authors use this property to construct a sound sequential peeling algorithm for general graphs. This gives the pairwise tests a role in recovering larger structures, rather than restricting their use to isolated two-variable problems.

The paper also proposes a heuristic for small graphs, which shows strong empirical performance. Evaluations on synthetic data from varied generating models show improvements over prior work, and the algorithms are additionally tested on real datasets. The contribution combines an identifiability result for larger causal graphs, a sound algorithm built on the ancestry property, and an empirically evaluated heuristic.
icml-2022-entropic-causal-inference-grap.tldr: Entropic causal inference extends from two variables to larger graphs by using pairwise tests to establish ancestral relationships.

paragraphs: Adaptive test-time defenses perform optimization when processing inputs, with the aim of improving resistance to adversarial manipulation. This paper examines whether that additional adaptation delivers stronger image classification defenses. It first categorizes these approaches and discusses the potential advantages and drawbacks of adapting during inference.

The authors then conduct careful case studies of a representative selection of recent adaptive defenses. None of the evaluated methods significantly improves on static defenses under their evaluation. Some reduce the robustness of the underlying static model while also requiring more computation at inference, so the additional optimization does not reliably translate into a security benefit in these cases.

The authors nevertheless regard adaptation at test time as a promising research direction. They contribute concrete recommendations for evaluating such methods, extending an existing adversarial-defense checklist with steps specific to adaptation. The paper’s message is grounded in the evaluated defenses: their results call for stronger assessment of claimed robustness gains while leaving open the development of more effective adaptive methods.
icml-2022-evaluating-the-adversarial-rob.tldr: Case studies find no significant robustness gains from the evaluated adaptive test-time defenses and motivate more targeted evaluation practices.

paragraphs: Many explanation methods need a label to decide which model output to explain. Unsupervised and self-supervised models often produce representation vectors instead, whose individual coordinates have no obvious meaning. Selecting a coordinate to interpret therefore becomes a problem before an explanation method can even be applied.

This paper introduces label-free versions of feature importance and example importance. Feature importance highlights input features that influence the representation constructed at inference time. Example importance highlights influential training examples. Together, these extensions provide two ways to investigate representation formation without requiring a labeled output as the explanation target.

The authors show that the extensions can be implemented as simple wrappers around many existing importance methods. They demonstrate the approach through qualitative and quantitative comparisons of representation spaces from autoencoders trained on different unsupervised tasks. The contribution makes established explanation techniques usable in a setting where meaningful output labels are unavailable, while preserving the distinction between explaining input features and explaining training-example influence.
icml-2022-label-free-explainability-for-.tldr: Label-free wrappers extend feature and training-example importance methods to explain representations learned without labels.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning methods are often thought to succeed at learning from few examples because they acquire representations shared across tasks. This paper gives a theoretical account of that explanation for MAML, ANIL, and their first-order approximations. It investigates both whether these methods recover a shared representation and what drives that recovery.

The proof applies in a multi-task linear representation learning setting. Within that setting, the methods recover the ground-truth representation at an exponentially fast rate. This establishes a concrete representation-learning capability for the analyzed algorithms, giving mathematical support to an explanation previously motivated by empirical evidence.

The analysis identifies adaptation of the final model layer as the driving mechanism. That adaptation uses diversity across tasks to improve the representation in all relevant directions. The result connects task-specific adjustment to shared learning: adapting the final layer helps expose information needed to recover the common representation. Its theoretical scope is the stated linear setting, where the authors rigorously characterize this mechanism.
icml-2022-maml-and-anil-provably-learn-r.tldr: In a multi-task linear setting, MAML and ANIL provably recover shared representations through final-layer adaptation that exploits task diversity.

paragraphs: Distributions over discrete sets describe both how often individual elements occur and how elements appear together. A model of shopping carts, for example, can capture relationships among products. When populations or conditions change, a pretrained generative model may no longer match the desired distribution.

This paper develops a framework for adapting such models to target marginal constraints, including possibly counterfactual targets. It reuses learned modules to preserve correlations among set elements while adjusting the components responsible for matching those constraints. The approach aims to retain useful learned structure without retraining an entire generative model from the beginning.

The authors instantiate the framework for latent-variable, autoregressive, and energy-based models, providing efficient constrained optimization solutions in primal or dual form. Experiments use synthetic data and real e-commerce and electronic health record datasets. The results show practical alignment with target marginal constraints under distribution shift. This supports modular adaptation as a sampling- and computation-efficient way to update selected distributional properties while retaining learned dependencies.
icml-2022-marginal-distribution-adaptati.tldr: Modular adaptation updates discrete-set generative models to match target marginals while reusing learned correlations.

paragraphs: Parallel k-means algorithms must balance solution quality, memory, and the number of communication rounds. For general inputs, earlier work gives conditional evidence against obtaining a constant-factor approximation in fewer than logarithmically many rounds. This paper investigates whether structurally stable inputs allow faster algorithms.

Its assumption is perturbation resilience: the optimal clusters stay unchanged when pairwise distances are multiplied by factors within a specified range. For inputs with resilience proportional to a parameter alpha, the authors give a fully scalable algorithm using a constant number of rounds and achieving a 1 + epsilon approximation. Its total space depends on alpha, dimension, and the requested approximation accuracy.

They also obtain an exact optimal solution in a constant number of rounds when each machine has sufficiently more memory than k, specifically at least k times a polynomial factor in the number of points. The findings show how stability assumptions can bypass obstacles associated with general inputs. The stronger exact-solution guarantee additionally relies on the stated per-machine memory condition.
icml-2022-massively-parallel-k-means-clu.tldr: Perturbation resilience enables constant-round parallel k-means approximation, with exact clustering under an additional per-machine memory condition.

paragraphs: A face recognition model can perform well overall while treating gender groups unevenly. This paper addresses both measuring that disparity and reducing it. The authors introduce two metrics, BFAR and BFRR, intended to reflect the deployment needs of face recognition systems more closely.

Their mitigation method transforms the embeddings produced by a pretrained recognition network. A shallow neural network learns this transformation using a Fair von Mises-Fisher loss, motivated by the geometry of the representations. Its hyperparameters account for within-class variability for each gender, with the aim of giving disadvantaged subgroups more expressive representations.

Experiments across several datasets show that carefully selecting these hyperparameters significantly reduces gender bias. The authors also observe an empirical correlation between the hyperparameters and their fairness metrics. This links the representation adjustment to the disparities the metrics measure, making parameter selection a substantive part of the approach. The stated outcome is reduced bias through post-processing pretrained embeddings, with improvements demonstrated empirically.
icml-2022-mitigating-gender-bias-in-face.tldr: A shallow transformation of pretrained face embeddings reduces measured gender bias through a carefully tuned Fair von Mises-Fisher loss.

paragraphs: CountSketch compresses vectors using randomized linear measurements while supporting recovery of entries that contribute a substantial share of the vector’s squared magnitude. This paper asks what happens when later inputs depend on answers to earlier queries. Such adaptive inputs arise through feedback and adversarial interaction.

The authors show that the classic CountSketch estimator is vulnerable: an attack can succeed with a number of queries on the order of the sketch size. This exposes a difference between using a randomized sketch on inputs independent of its answers and repeatedly interacting with it in a way that responds to those answers.

They then propose a robust estimator for a slightly modified sketch that supports a number of queries quadratic in the sketch size. For recovering k heavy hitters, the stated improvement over earlier generic robustness wrappers is a factor of the square root of k. The contribution shows that a design tailored to CountSketch can improve adaptive robustness beyond what those black-box approaches provide.
icml-2022-on-the-robustness-of-countsket.tldr: A tailored CountSketch estimator supports quadratically many adaptive queries in sketch size, improving on prior generic robustness approaches.

paragraphs: Sampling a massive data stream reduces the amount of material that later analysis must process. In genomic applications with severe class imbalance, however, uniform sampling can leave rare groups poorly represented. The challenge is to preserve diversity without adding overhead that makes high-throughput processing impractical.

This paper proposes a one-pass sampling routine that maintains an online representation of the data distribution. It uses that representation as a prefilter, preferentially retaining elements likely to belong to rare groups. The selection process therefore responds to the observed distribution, aiming to produce a sample that is useful despite highly unequal group frequencies.

Across several genomic analysis tasks, the authors report substantial downstream speedups without sacrificing result quality. They also report that their algorithm is twice as fast and uses 1,000 times less memory than the compared coreset, reservoir, and sketch-based alternatives. These findings support diversity-aware sampling as a practical preprocessing step for large genomic streams, with the broader usefulness for streaming applications presented as an expectation.
icml-2022-one-pass-diversified-sampling-.tldr: An efficient streaming prefilter favors rare groups, accelerating genomic analyses while preserving the reported quality of their results.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering starts with pairwise recommendations: some pairs should share a cluster, while others should be separated. Its objective is to minimize disagreements with those recommendations. This paper studies the online setting, where new vertices arrive over time and a clustering must be maintained as the input grows.

The additional concern is recourse, meaning how often an existing vertex changes clusters. Updating assignments may help maintain an approximate solution, but repeatedly moving the same vertex makes the clustering less consistent over time. The authors design an algorithm that bounds each vertex’s recourse logarithmically in the worst case while maintaining an approximate clustering.

A matching lower bound shows that the recourse guarantee is tight in the studied setting. Experiments on real-world data also show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. The contribution combines a theoretical account of how much reassignment is required with an algorithm that reaches that bound, addressing stability of membership alongside the clustering objective.
icml-2022-online-and-consistent-correlat.tldr: An online correlation clustering algorithm achieves a tight logarithmic bound on how often each vertex changes clusters.

paragraphs: Average-case optimization analysis can describe convergence more precisely than worst-case guarantees, but earlier approaches require detailed knowledge of the expected eigenvalue distribution of a problem’s random matrix. This paper asks how much of that distribution must actually be known to characterize long-run average complexity.

The authors show that the concentration of eigenvalues near the distribution’s edges determines asymptotic average complexity. Approximate knowledge of that concentration offers a middle ground between a coarse worst-case description and complete knowledge of the spectral distribution. The relevant information is therefore concentrated in particular parts of the spectrum for the asymptotic question being studied.

The paper introduces a Generalized Chebyshev method that is asymptotically optimal under an assumption about this edge concentration. It is globally optimal when the expected spectral distribution is a Beta distribution. Comparisons with classical methods also establish that Nesterov’s method is universally nearly optimal asymptotically in the average-case context considered. These results clarify both the information needed for analysis and the conditions supporting algorithmic optimality.
icml-2022-only-tails-matter-average-case.tldr: Spectral edge concentration determines asymptotic average optimization complexity and supports optimality results under stated distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows connect independent latent variables to generated samples through an invertible transformation. This exact correspondence does not by itself explain the higher-level relationship between latent variation and sample structure. The paper studies that relationship geometrically, using principal manifolds and contours.

The authors introduce principal component flows, or PCFs, whose contours coincide with their principal manifolds. These models can use any flow architecture and are trained through regularized maximum likelihood. They also introduce an injective variant, iPCF, that is more efficient to train than regular injective flows. The construction connects the organization of the flow’s latent variables to geometric structure in the samples.

Experiments show PCFs and iPCFs learning principal manifolds across several datasets. PCFs can estimate densities on all their principal manifolds, and the authors demonstrate density estimation for data lying on a manifold with variable dimensionality. They identify this capability as unavailable in existing normalizing flows. The contribution therefore combines a geometric characterization with a model class that supports richer manifold-based density estimation.
icml-2022-principal-component-flows-8eb0.tldr: Principal component flows align flow contours with principal manifolds and enable density estimation on manifolds of variable dimensionality.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how internal units in pretrained Transformer language models guide generation. Using a Product of Experts formulation, the authors describe units that detect concepts in the input and help condition the generated text. They develop a procedure for identifying these units and activating them during inference.

The experiments show that activating very few units can steer generation: one reported example uses just three units in a model with 345 million parameters. The method requires neither fine-tuning nor extra parameters and also works for fine-grained concepts involving homographs, where the same written form can carry different meanings.

The authors additionally use self-conditioning to address gender bias in generated output, achieving gender parity in all evaluated contexts. Compared with FUDGE and PPLM-BoW, their approach reaches parity with lower perplexity and a better Self-BLEU score. These results support both a lightweight control mechanism and an interpretation of how existing concept-sensitive units contribute to generation, with the parity finding scoped to the evaluated contexts.
icml-2022-self-conditioning-pre-trained-.tldr: Activating a small number of existing concept-sensitive units steers language generation without fine-tuning or added parameters.

paragraphs: Training datasets sometimes contain information unavailable when a model is deployed, such as the identity of the person who supplied a label. This paper argues that such privileged information can help explain noisy labels. Accounting for information associated with the labeling process can reduce the harmful effect of that noise on supervised learning.

The proposed method, TRAM, transfers knowledge learned with privileged information through shared neural-network weights. At test time, it approximately marginalizes over that information, accounting for its possible values without requiring it as an input. The design connects the richer training setting to the more restricted information available during deployment.

The authors report minimal additional training overhead and the same test-time cost as a model that does not use privileged information. TRAM performs strongly on CIFAR-10H, ImageNet, and Civil Comments. The contribution is a simple method for exploiting training-only features to handle label noise while keeping inference practical when those features are absent.
icml-2022-transfer-and-marginalize-expla.tldr: TRAM uses training-only information to account for label noise without increasing test-time computation.

paragraphs: Learning to classify strings correctly during training does not necessarily prepare a recurrent neural network for systematic distribution shifts. This paper investigates that issue through regular languages. It compares directly mapping strings to labels with learning the structure of the deterministic finite-state automaton that recognizes the language.

The authors prove that the compositional strategy generalizes significantly better in their theoretical comparison. In experiments, they implement the idea with an auxiliary task: predicting the intermediate automaton states visited while processing a string. That task supplies supervision about the sequence of internal decisions involved in recognizing the language.

The empirical results support the proposal that auxiliary tasks can enable robust generalization. They also reveal an important qualification: the end-to-end recurrent network performs substantially better than its theoretical lower bound, indicating some capacity for robust generalization. The study therefore supports structural supervision while acknowledging that direct end-to-end learning can generalize more successfully than the lower bound alone might suggest.
icml-2022-understanding-robust-generaliz.tldr: Predicting intermediate automaton states helps recurrent networks generalize regular languages under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Deep Latent Particles represents an image through a collection of compact latent particles. Each particle carries a spatial location and features describing its surrounding region. This separates where visual content is located from what that content looks like, giving the representation an explicit spatial organization.

The method learns these representations through a variational autoencoder approach. It introduces a prior over particle positions based on a spatial-Softmax architecture and modifies the training objective using an idea inspired by Chamfer distance between particles. These choices shape how particle locations and local appearance information are learned together from visual inputs.

The authors demonstrate uses in unsupervised keypoint detection, image manipulation, and video prediction for scenes containing multiple moving objects. The probabilistic formulation also provides uncertainty estimates for particle locations, which can support model selection. The findings show that the particle representation can serve several downstream tasks while expressing uncertainty about where its visual components are located.
icml-2022-unsupervised-image-representat.tldr: Deep Latent Particles learns spatially organized image representations that separate position from appearance and estimate location uncertainty.
